what_its_for: Tinidazole is an antibiotic used to treat certain infections caused by bacteria or parasites. It is commonly used to treat infections in the stomach and intestines (such as giardia and amebiasis), vaginal infections (such as bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis), and certain other bacterial infections. It works by killing the harmful organisms causing your infection.
how_to_take: Take tinidazole by mouth with food to help prevent an upset stomach. Swallow the tablet whole if possible. If you have trouble swallowing the tablet, you may crush it and mix it with a teaspoon of artificial cherry syrup to make it easier to take. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Finish all of your medication even if you start feeling better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: Your dose will depend on the type of infection you have and your age or weight. Common doses for adults are usually a single large dose (2 grams) taken one time, or a smaller dose taken once daily for several days. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take and for how long. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are only taking a single one-time dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store tinidazole at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the package. Dispose of unused medication safely — ask your pharmacist about a medication take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking tinidazole and for at least 3 days after your last dose. Mixing alcohol with tinidazole can cause a very unpleasant reaction including nausea, vomiting, flushing, fast heartbeat, and stomach cramps. Avoid alcohol in all forms including beer, wine, liquor, and products that contain alcohol such as certain mouthwashes and cough syrups. Also avoid activities that require alertness, such as driving or operating machinery, if you feel dizzy or confused while taking this medication.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: seizures or tremors, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, severe dizziness or confusion, signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, severe stomach pain or diarrhea, dark or unusual colored urine, or yellowing of your skin or eyes. Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve after finishing your medication or if they get worse.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a day or two of starting tinidazole. However, it is very important to take the full course of medication as prescribed, even if you feel better sooner. Stopping early may allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat. If you do not notice any improvement after a few days, let your doctor know.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tinidazole should NOT be used during the first trimester (first 3 months) of pregnancy. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant before using this medication. Breastfeeding: You should not breastfeed while taking tinidazole and for at least 3 days after your last dose, as the medication can pass into breast milk. Children: Tinidazole can be used in children for certain infections, but the dose will be based on the child's weight. Follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects. Your doctor may adjust your dose if needed. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, tell your doctor before taking tinidazole, as the medication is processed by the liver.
